topic: Text and speech solutions in Foundry

notes.front: What is Azure Speech (Azure Speech in Foundry Tools)?
notes.back: The Foundry Tool that provides speech to text, text to speech and other speech capabilities through a Microsoft Foundry resource.
notes.explanation: It also translates spoken audio and runs live voice conversations.
notes.example: Like a studio with a transcriber, a narrator and an interpreter on call, all in the cloud.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “What is Azure Speech?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools provides speech to text, text to speech, and other capabilities through a Microsoft Foundry resource. You can transcribe speech to text with high accuracy, produce natural-sounding text-to-speech voices, translate spoken audio, and conduct live AI voice conversations.

notes.front: What is the Speech SDK?
notes.back: A software development kit that exposes many Azure Speech capabilities for building speech-enabled applications.
notes.explanation: It is available in many programming languages and on all platforms.
notes.example: Like a toolkit of ready-made parts that lets an app listen and talk.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Integration of Azure Speech in your application” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This SDK exposes many of the Azure Speech capabilities that you can use to develop speech-enabled applications. The Speech SDK is available in many programming languages and across all platforms.

notes.front: What is the Speech CLI?
notes.back: A command-line tool for using Azure Speech without writing any code.
notes.explanation: Most Speech SDK features are available in it, and some advanced features are simpler there.
notes.example: Like using a microwave’s preset buttons instead of writing your own cooking program.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Speech?”, “Integration of Azure Speech in your application” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With this command-line tool, you can use Azure Speech without having to write any code. Most features in the Speech SDK are available in the Speech CLI, and some advanced features and customizations are simplified in the Speech CLI.

notes.front: In Foundry, what are audio completions?
notes.back: Chat completions with an audio modality, so a model can take spoken prompts and reply with generated speech.
notes.explanation: Spoken audio can be both the prompt and the response.
notes.example: Like leaving a voice message for an assistant and getting a spoken reply back.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Audio generation with chat completions”, “Audio generation with chat completions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Models that support audio inputs and outputs allow you to generate spoken audio responses to prompts and use audio inputs to prompt the model.

notes.front: What is the Realtime API?
notes.back: An Azure OpenAI interface for low-latency “speech in, speech out” conversations between a user and a model.
notes.explanation: It suits live interactions such as customer support agents, voice assistants and real-time translators.
notes.example: Like a phone call with the model rather than an exchange of letters.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The GPT Realtime API is designed to handle real-time, low-latency conversational interactions. It's a great fit for use cases involving live interactions between a user and a model, such as customer support agents, voice assistants, and real-time translators.

notes.front: For the Realtime API, what is WebRTC?
notes.back: A connection method for client-side applications such as web, mobile and browser apps, at about 100 ms latency.
notes.explanation: Its latency is the lowest of the connection methods in Microsoft’s table.
notes.example: Like a video call in your browser: the audio flows straight to and from the page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “Connection methods” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **WebRTC** | Client-side applications | ~100ms | Web apps, mobile apps, browser-based experiences |

notes.front: For the Realtime API, what is WebSocket?
notes.back: A connection method for server-to-server use, such as backend services and custom middleware, at about 200 ms latency.
notes.explanation: Backend services, batch processing and custom middleware are its typical users.
notes.example: Like a permanent phone line between two offices, rather than a caller’s mobile.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “Connection methods” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **WebSocket** | Server-to-server | ~200ms | Backend services, batch processing, custom middleware |

notes.front: What is Voice Live (the Voice Live API)?
notes.back: An interface for speech-to-speech voice agents that integrates speech recognition, generative AI and text to speech into one.
notes.explanation: It removes the need to orchestrate those components yourself.
notes.example: Like hiring one interpreter who listens, thinks and speaks, instead of three people passing notes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Voice Live API for real-time voice agents”, “What is the Voice Live API?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The API is designed for developers seeking scalable and efficient voice-driven experiences as it eliminates the need to manually orchestrate multiple components. By integrating speech recognition, generative AI, and text-to-speech functionalities into a single, unified interface, it provides an end-to-end solution for creating seamless experiences.

notes.front: What is a voice-based prompt agent?
notes.back: A managed Foundry agent for real-time spoken conversations, configured with a model, instructions, audio settings and tools.
notes.explanation: Foundry uses Voice Live for speech recognition, turn taking, the model interaction and speech synthesis.
notes.example: Like a prompt agent that answers the phone instead of a chat window.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Foundry Agent Service?”, “Voice-based prompt agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Voice-based prompt agents are managed agents for real-time, spoken conversations. Configure a model, instructions, audio settings, optional greeting, and tools in the agent definition. Foundry Agent Service manages the agent lifecycle and uses Voice Live for speech recognition, turn taking, model interaction, and speech synthesis.

notes.front: In speech translation, what is Live Interpreter?
notes.back: A fuller real-time speech translation experience for conversations that identifies the spoken language without you setting it.
notes.explanation: It delivers low-latency speech-to-speech translation in a natural voice that keeps the speaker’s style and tone.
notes.example: Like a personal interpreter who hears whichever language you switch to and keeps up.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “Live interpreter” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It continuously identifies the language being spoken without requiring you to set an input language and delivers low latency speech-to-speech translation in a natural voice that preserves the speaker's style and tone.

notes.front: How can you try several Azure Language features without writing code?
notes.back: In Microsoft Foundry, a web-based platform.
notes.explanation: The alternative is the quickstart, which sends requests with a client library or as direct web requests, so it needs code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is key phrase extraction in Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Next steps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Foundry is a web-based platform that lets you use several Language features without needing to write code.

notes.front: In the typical workflow for a preconfigured Azure Language feature, what is the first step?
notes.back: Create an Azure Language in Foundry Tools resource, which gives you a key and an endpoint.
notes.explanation: The key and endpoint then authenticate every request you send.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Typical workflow (Azure Language)”, “Typical workflow” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Create an Azure Language in Foundry Tools resource, which grants you access to the features offered by Language. It generates a password (called a key) and an endpoint URL that you use to authenticate API requests.

notes.front: What happens to Azure Language Studio on 20 March 2027?
notes.back: It retires and migrates to Microsoft Foundry.
notes.explanation: All its capabilities and future enhancements will be available in Microsoft Foundry.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Explore Microsoft Foundry SDKs and endpoints (Foundry Tools)”, “Language endpoints” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On March 20, 2027, Azure Language Studio will retire and migrate to Microsoft Foundry; all capabilities and future enhancements will be available in Microsoft Foundry.

notes.front: Can the Chat Completion interface be used for a non-chat task such as sentiment analysis?
notes.back: Yes. It is optimised for multi-turn chat but also works for non-chat scenarios.
notes.explanation: You write a prompt that asks the model to perform the analysis.
notes.source: Microsoft, “How to work with prompt engineering and the Chat Completion API”, “Non chat scenarios” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: While the Chat Completion API is optimized to work with multi-turn conversations, it also can be used for non chat scenarios. For example, for a sentiment analysis scenario, you might use the following prompt:

notes.front: Which input and output modalities do the audio preview chat models support?
notes.back: Text, audio, and text plus audio.
notes.explanation: So a model can, for example, take audio in and return text for transcription, or return text and audio.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Audio generation with chat completions”, “Audio generation with chat completions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Modalities supported in `gpt-4o-audio-preview` and `gpt-4o-mini-audio-preview` models include: text, audio, and text + audio.

notes.front: What is the largest audio file you can send to an audio completion?
notes.back: 20 megabytes.
notes.explanation: It is one of the input requirements, alongside the supported voices and output formats.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Audio generation with chat completions”, “Input requirements” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The maximum audio file size is 20 MB.

notes.front: How does the Realtime API relate to the audio completions model?
notes.back: It uses the same underlying audio model, but is optimised for low-latency, real-time audio interactions.
notes.explanation: Choose the Realtime API when the conversation is live.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Audio generation with chat completions”, “Supported models” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Realtime API uses the same underlying GPT-4o audio model as the completions API, but is optimized for low-latency, real-time audio interactions.

notes.front: Besides WebRTC and WebSocket, what is the third way to connect to the Realtime API?
notes.back: Session initiation protocol, for telephony integration.
notes.explanation: All three send audio to the model and receive audio responses in real time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “Connection methods” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use the Realtime API via WebRTC, session initiation protocol (SIP), or WebSocket to send audio input to the model and receive audio responses in real time.

notes.front: Which Realtime API connection method does Microsoft recommend in most cases?
notes.back: WebRTC.
notes.explanation: It is recommended for low-latency real-time audio streaming.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “Connection methods” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In most cases, we recommend using the WebRTC API for low-latency real-time audio streaming.

notes.front: Do you need to deploy a generative AI model to use Voice Live?
notes.back: Not for its natively supported models: Voice Live is fully managed. A few other models need your own deployment.
notes.explanation: You provide audio input and receive audio output, avatar visuals and action triggers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Voice Live API for real-time voice agents”, “What is the Voice Live API?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Developers provide audio input and receive audio output, avatar visuals, and action triggers—all with minimal latency. You don't need to deploy or manage any generative AI models, as the API handles the underlying infrastructure.

notes.front: How does a client connect to a voice-based prompt agent?
notes.back: Over a real-time WebSocket, instead of sending individual text requests.
notes.explanation: Setup and supported client languages are in the voice agent quickstart.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Foundry Agent Service?”, “Voice-based prompt agents” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You connect to the agent over a real-time WebSocket instead of sending individual text requests.

notes.front: Which Foundry Tools endpoint form does standard speech to text use?
notes.back: `https://<YOUR-RESOURCE-REGION>.stt.speech.microsoft.com`
notes.explanation: Text to speech uses a matching tts address in the same region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Explore Microsoft Foundry SDKs and endpoints (Foundry Tools)”, “Speech Endpoints” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Speech to Text (Standard)|`https://<YOUR-RESOURCE-REGION>.stt.speech.microsoft.com`| |Text to Speech (Neural)|`https://<YOUR-RESOURCE-REGION>.tts.speech.microsoft.com`|

notes.front: Through which tools is real-time speech to text available?
notes.back: The Speech SDK, the Speech CLI, and direct web requests to speech to text, for short audio.
notes.explanation: All three give real-time transcription; they differ in how you call them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Real-time transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Real-time speech to text is available via the Speech SDK, the Speech CLI, and Speech to text REST API for short audio.

notes.front: A call centre wants agents to see a live transcript of each customer call while it happens. What should the developer build with?
notes.back: Real-time speech to text through the Speech SDK.
notes.choices:
A) Batch transcription through the web interface
B) Real-time speech to text through the Speech SDK
C) Text to speech
D) Image Analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A processes stored recordings later. C produces speech. D analyses pictures.
notes.explanation: Real-time transcription assists customer service representatives during calls.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Real-time transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Providing real-time transcription to assist customer service representatives.

notes.front: A market research firm must transcribe 5,000 recorded focus groups, and a developer wants a command-line route with no code. Which fits?
notes.back: Batch transcription with the Speech CLI.
notes.choices:
A) Real-time transcription with a microphone
B) Batch transcription with the Speech CLI
C) Voice Live
D) Audio completions, one file at a time
notes.choicesExplained: A needs live audio. C is for live voice agents. D is not meant for large volumes of stored audio.
notes.explanation: The Speech CLI supports batch transcription and needs no code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech to text?”, “Batch transcription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Speech CLI: Supports both real-time and batch transcription, making it easy to manage transcription tasks.

notes.front: A council wants a spoken helpline bot without building its own pipeline of recognition, model and synthesis. Which fits best?
notes.back: Voice Live.
notes.choices:
A) Batch transcription
B) Voice Live
C) SSML on its own
D) Image Analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A transcribes stored audio. C only shapes synthesised speech. D analyses images.
notes.explanation: Voice Live combines speech recognition, generative AI and text to speech in one managed interface.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Voice Live API for real-time voice agents”, “Compare Voice Live API with other speech-to-speech solutions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Voice Live API is an alternative to orchestrating multiple components such as speech recognition, generative AI, and text to speech.

notes.front: A browser-based tutoring app streams the learner’s voice straight to a realtime model. Which connection method fits?
notes.back: WebRTC.
notes.choices:
A) WebRTC
B) WebSocket
C) Session initiation protocol
D) Batch transcription
notes.choicesExplained: B is for server-to-server connections. C is for telephony. D is not a realtime connection.
notes.explanation: WebRTC suits client-side web and mobile apps and gives the lowest latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “GPT Realtime API for speech and audio”, “Connection methods” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In most cases, we recommend using the WebRTC API for low-latency real-time audio streaming.

notes.front: A kiosk lets visitors ask a question aloud and hear a spoken answer from a chat model; latency need not be very low. Which capability fits?
notes.back: Audio completions.
notes.choices:
A) Audio completions
B) Image Analysis
C) Live Interpreter
D) Batch transcription only
notes.choicesExplained: B analyses images. C translates between languages. D gives text, not a spoken answer.
notes.explanation: Audio-enabled chat models accept spoken prompts and generate spoken responses.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Audio generation with chat completions”, “Audio generation with chat completions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Models that support audio inputs and outputs allow you to generate spoken audio responses to prompts and use audio inputs to prompt the model.

notes.front: A bank’s voice agent needs a wide choice of Azure voices and a phrase list for its product names. Which voice-agent architecture fits?
notes.back: The cascaded text model.
notes.choices:
A) Native speech-to-speech
B) The cascaded text model
C) Batch transcription
D) Image generation
notes.choicesExplained: A is optimised for latency, with voices depending on the model. C and D are not voice-agent architectures.
notes.explanation: The cascade gives broader Azure voice choices and explicit control over transcription and phrase lists.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Foundry Agent Service?”, “Cascaded text model” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This architecture provides broader text-model and Azure voice choices. It also provides explicit control over transcription, phrase lists, turn detection, and interim responses, but each stage contributes to end-to-end latency.

notes.front: In a business meeting, speakers switch between Spanish and German, and nobody wants to set the input language. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Live Interpreter.
notes.choices:
A) Standard speech translation with a fixed source language
B) Live Interpreter
C) Text to speech
D) Custom speech
notes.choicesExplained: A needs the source language specified. C only speaks text. D improves recognition accuracy but does not translate.
notes.explanation: It identifies the spoken language continuously and handles language switching in one session.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “Live interpreter” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Language switching. Handle multiple spoken languages in the same session without restarting.

notes.front: An English webinar needs live French and German text in one speech translation call. Is that possible without extra services?
notes.back: Yes. Speech translation can output two target languages in a single call.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, two target languages in one call
B) No, only one target language per call
C) Only after training custom speech
D) Only with batch transcription
notes.choicesExplained: B understates the limit. C and D are unrelated to the number of target languages.
notes.explanation: Beyond two languages you need a multi-service resource or separate translation services.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is speech translation?”, “Multiple target languages translation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: the Speech service directly offers the ability for you to translate the input language into two target languages.

notes.front: An analyst wants to try key phrase extraction on some reviews before any developer is involved. What should she use?
notes.back: Microsoft Foundry, which lets her use Language features without code.
notes.choices:
A) Microsoft Foundry
B) The Speech CLI
C) A hosted agent
D) Batch transcription
notes.choicesExplained: B works with speech, not text analysis. C requires code. D transcribes audio.
notes.explanation: Foundry is a web-based platform for trying several Language features without writing code.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is key phrase extraction in Azure Language in Foundry Tools?”, “Next steps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Foundry is a web-based platform that lets you use several Language features without needing to write code.

notes.front: How does a native speech-to-speech voice agent differ from a cascaded text model?
notes.back: Native uses one realtime speech model for lower latency; the cascade chains recognition, a text model and synthesis for more choice and control.
notes.explanation: Each stage in the cascade adds to end-to-end latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Foundry Agent Service?”, “Native speech-to-speech” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This architecture is optimized for natural, low-latency conversation. The realtime model handles spoken input and output directly.
